paragraphs.text: Date of hearing: 02.11.2026. Appellants by: M/s Sheikh Naveed Shahryar, Safina Safdar and Nadia Iffat, Advocates. Respondents by: Already ex parte vide order dated 15.09.2026. Mr. Muhammad Saad Bin Ghazi, Assistant Advocate General and Mr. Muhammad Zain Qazi, Assistant Attorney General on Court’s call. MUHAMMAD SAJID MEHMOOD SETHI, J.- Through instant appeal, the appellants have assailed judgment and decree dated 24.03.2026 passed by learned Additional District Judge, Sargodha, whereby appeal filed by respondents was accepted, the judgment and decree of the learned trial Court dated 14.05.2015 were set aside, and the suit for specific performance, instituted by the appellants, was dismissed with costs.

Briefly, the appellants instituted a suit for specific performance on 23.04.2003 in respect of certain shops situated in Sargodha, of which they claimed to be tenants. Their case was that Ch. Deen Muhammad, predecessor-in-interest of the respondents, who was residing in the United States, visited Pakistan in May 2000 and, in view of three pending ejectment petitions against them, agreed to sell the shops orally on 03.05.2000, which arrangement was reduced into writing on 04.05.2000 (Ex.P-8). A sum of Rs.500,000/- was allegedly paid as earnest money against receipt (Ex.P-7). It was further pleaded that the vendor appeared before the Rent Controller on 04.05.2000 and withdrew the ejectment petitions through compromise (Ex.P-4 to Ex.P-6). On the same date, he also executed a general power of attorney (Ex.P-16) in favour of Sheikh Muhammad Nazir Kausar. The appellants claimed to have issued legal notices (Ex.P-9 to Ex.P-11), calling upon the vendor to perform his contractual obligations, and also appeared before the Sub-Registrar, Sargodha, for execution of the sale deed (Ex.P-12), wherein their attendance was recorded. The respondents contested the suit, denying execution of the agreement and receipt of earnest money. After framing issues and recording evidence, learned trial Court decreed the suit vide judgment and decree dated 14.05.2015. The respondents preferred an appeal, which was initially allowed on 04.09.2018, and the matter was remanded to the trial Court after framing additional issue No.8-A. The appellants challenged the remand order through FAO No.241375/2018, which was allowed by this Court on 04.02.2026, setting aside the remand order and directing the learned Additional District Judge to decide the appeal afresh. Upon reconsideration, the learned appellate Court, vide impugned judgment and decree dated 24.03.2026, accepted the appeal and dismissed the suit. Hence, this appeal.

Learned counsel for the appellants contends that the impugned judgment is contrary to law and the evidence available on record, particularly as the learned appellate Court reversed the findings of the trial Court without properly appreciating the testimony of the scribe and marginal witnesses, as well as the contemporaneous documentary evidence. He further contends that the appeal before the learned Additional District Judge was decided on merits despite absence of the appellants before that Court, in violation of Order XLI Rule 17, C.P.C. Reliance is placed upon Sazia Sultana v. Razia Begum (PLD 2003 Lahore 27). He also submits that the controversy relates to immovable property involving an Overseas Pakistani and, therefore, falls within the ambit of the Punjab Establishment of Special Courts (Overseas Pakistanis Property) Act, 2025, rendering the jurisdiction of the ordinary appellate forum subject to the special statutory arrangement.

The questions for determination are: (A) whether the appeal could be decided on merits in the absence of the appellants before the first appellate Court; (B) whether the 2025 Act affects the forum in which this litigation must proceed; (C) whether the appellate judgment reflects a proper appraisal of the evidence and satisfies Order XLI, Rule 31, C.P.C.; and (D) what order is appropriate in second appellate jurisdiction. A. Decision of an appeal on merits in the absence of the appellant

Order XLI, Rule 17, C.P.C. treats the absence of an appellant and the absence of a respondent differently. Where the appellant does not appear when the appeal is called on for hearing, sub-rule (1) empowers the Court to dismiss the appeal for default; it does not empower the Court to decide it on merits. Where the appellant appears and the respondent does not, sub-rule (2) requires the appeal to be heard ex parte, subject to due service. The distinction rests on a sound principle: a Court cannot adjudicate on merits a grievance that the party who raised it has not chosen to press, whereas a respondent who stays away may fairly be heard in his absence. The Supreme Court has accordingly held that an appellate Court cannot decide an appeal on merits in the absence of the appellant. It has further been emphasized that the appeal must actually have been fixed for hearing before sub-rule (1) can be invoked. Reference can be made to M. Muhammad Sadiq and another v. Punjab Road Transport Board, Lahore through Managing Director (1991 SCMR 2321), Messrs Suhail Printing Press v. Syed Aley Eba Zaidi (2005 SCMR 882) and Abdul Rehman and another v. Syed Jaffar Hussain Razvi (deceased) through LRs (2026 SCMR 1316).

The absence that matters is that of the appellant before the Court concerned, not that of the appellant in later proceedings. The respondents in this appeal were the appellants before the first appellate Court. The inquiry is therefore whether, on the date the appeal was decided, they or their counsel was absent when it was called on for hearing, and whether it had been fixed for that date. The principle in Sazia Sultana, on which the appellants rely, operates only to that extent. The record suggests that the appeal was fixed on the fateful day and none was present on behalf of appellants, as duly noted in the first page of the impugned judgment of learned Appellate Court. The impugned judgment was therefore rendered without lawful authority. B. The Act of 2025 and the forum of adjudication

The 2025 Act (Act IX of 2025) came into force on 29.01.2025. Section 2(c) defines an “Overseas Pakistani” as a person holding a Pakistani passport, CNIC, NICOP, Pakistan Origin Card or OPF membership card, and living, working or studying abroad, permanently or temporarily, for more than 182 days in a tax year. Section 4(3) provides that, notwithstanding anything contained in the Code or any other law, all actions, suits, proceedings and matters connected therewith in which one or more of the parties are Overseas Pakistanis shall be heard and adjudicated exclusively by a Special Court. Section 13 deals with pending matters: under clause (a), pending suits and proceedings stand transferred to the Special Court, while under clause (b), all appeals and revisions in which any or all parties are Overseas Pakistanis, pending before any Court after commencement of the Act, stand transferred to the Special Bench or Benches of the concerned High Court. The statutory scheme thus distinguishes between original and appellate proceedings, and the transfer in each case takes effect by operation of law.

The appellants' case has throughout been that the vendor, Ch. Deen Muhammad, resided in the United States and executed the agreement during a visit to Pakistan, and the subject-matter is immovable property. The respondents, who claim through him as his legal representatives, have not controverted his status and are precluded before this Court. A legal representative stands in the shoes of the deceased and represents his estate. The dispute, though it has outlived the vendor, remains one concerning the immovable property of an Overseas Pakistani, in which the Act applies where “one or more” of the parties are Overseas Pakistanis. The Act is remedial legislation, intended to protect the property of Overseas Pakistanis, and its provisions are to be read so as to advance that object, not to defeat it by a narrow construction. The Special Bench, as the forum seized of the matter, remains competent to examine any jurisdictional fact under section 2(c) that may be disputed before it.

It is undisputed that the first appeal was pending before the learned Additional District Judge when the Act came into force on 29.01.2025. By virtue of section 13(b), it stood transferred to the Special Bench of this Court from that date, and the learned Additional District Judge thereafter had no jurisdiction to decide it. Jurisdiction is conferred by statute alone; it cannot be created or taken away by consent, waiver or acquiescence, and a decree passed without jurisdiction is a nullity, the invalidity of which may be raised at any stage as held in Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan (AIR 1954 SC 340). The judgment dated 24.03.2026 therefore cannot stand. Nor does this Court's earlier order dated 04.02.2026, directing a fresh decision of the appeal, alter the position, as a statutory transfer cannot be overridden by a direction that did not consider it. C. Appraisal of evidence and requirements of Order XLI, Rule 31, C.P.C.

The first appellate Court is the final Court of fact. Its decision is a continuation of the trial and must rest on an independent re-appraisal of the entire evidence. Order XLI, Rule 31, C.P.C. requires the judgment to state the points for determination, the decision on each and the reasons for it. Where a decree is reversed, the reasons must show why the trial Court's conclusions were not accepted, so that the parties and the higher forum can see that the mind of the Court was applied to the material. The appellate Court was free to differ from the trial Court, but not without such an appraisal. i). Execution of the agreement and payment of earnest money.

Under Article 117 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 burden of proving the agreement lay on the appellants, who asserted it. An agreement to sell immovable property that creates financial obligations falls within Article 17(2)(a) of the Order, and its execution, where denied, must be proved in the manner prescribed by Article 79. Reference can be made to Muhammad Humayun and others v. Shafqat Ali Nisar and others (2026 SCMR 1332). The Court was therefore required to determine whether PW-8 and PW-9 were the requisite attesting witnesses and whether, with PW-3 (the scribe), they proved execution in the manner the law requires. Their mere production was not sufficient. Payment of earnest money required independent proof, tested against the terms of Ex.P-7 and Ex.P-8, since a plaintiff seeking specific performance must establish both execution and payment of the earnest money or part consideration alleged, as held in Muhammad Ghaffar (deceased) through LRs and others v. Arif Muhammad (2023 SCMR 344). Oral evidence inconsistent with the written terms needs a proper plea and cogent support. The withdrawal of the ejectment petitions and the general power of attorney, both dated 04.05.2000, are relevant surrounding circumstances. They corroborate, but do not by themselves establish, the disputed sale, and must be weighed cumulatively with the oral evidence and the documents. ii). Comparison of signatures.

The learned appellate Court relied on the apparent dissimilarity between the signatures on Ex.P-7 and Ex.P-8 and those on Ex.P-16. Article 84 of the Order permits a Court to compare a disputed signature with one admitted or proved to be genuine. The Supreme Court has recognised that competence in the case reported as Mst. Nazeeran and others v. Ali Bux and others (2024 SCMR 1271), while also cautioning that visual comparison by a Court must be undertaken carefully and as an aid to the other evidence, not as a substitute for it. Reference can be made to Rehmat Ali Ismailia v. Khalid Mehmood (2004 SCMR 361) and Mrs. Tasneem Abbas v. Additional District Judge, Lahore and others (2026 SCMR 171). Comparison presupposes that the specimen is itself admitted or proved, and a Court that finds a dissimilarity should say why it is material, especially where the document is supported by the scribe and the marginal witnesses. The availability or absence of expert evidence is also a relevant consideration. Genuineness had to be decided on the whole of the evidence, not on comparison in isolation. iii). Discrepancies.

The appellate Court questioned the particulars of the alleged oral agreement of 03.05.2000 and the year recorded beneath the scribe's signature on the written agreement. The trial Court had treated the latter as a clerical error, since the document otherwise expressly bears the date 04.05.2000. Not every inconsistency invalidates a transaction. Only a discrepancy that goes to the root of the matter impairs credibility, and its materiality must be assessed against the pleadings, the documents and the surrounding circumstances. A Court that takes a contrary view must record why the discrepancy is material. The omission of particulars of the oral agreement cannot be considered apart from the written agreement, if its execution is established. iv). Readiness and willingness.

The appellants relied on the legal notices (Ex.P-9 to Ex.P-11), postal receipts, correspondence and their attendance before the Sub- Registrar (Ex.P-12). This evidence is relevant but not conclusive. Specific performance is a discretionary equitable remedy under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, to be exercised on settled judicial principles enunciated in Mst. Rehmat Begum v. Mehfooz Ahmed and others (PLD 2024 Supreme Court 1108), and under section 24(b) it cannot be enforced in favour of a person who has become incapable of performing, or has violated, an essential term that remained to be performed on his part. Equity aids the vigilant, and readiness, willingness and ability to perform must therefore be shown by the plaintiff's conduct throughout the proceedings. Reference can be made to Amjad Javed and another v. Maqsood Ahmad and others (2026 SCMR 1726). The Court had to examine the contractual terms and period, the appellants' financial capacity to pay the balance consideration, any tender or deposit, and their compliance with any direction to deposit the balance, which, if disregarded despite adequate opportunity, may weigh against the plaintiff. The returned notices bearing the endorsements “addressee deceased” and “non-availability” also had to be assessed against their dates and the date of the vendor's death.

The appellate judgment does not reflect an independent and comprehensive consideration of these interrelated questions. They concern execution of Ex.P-7 and Ex.P-8, payment of earnest money, the testimony of the scribe and marginal witnesses, the contemporaneous ejectment proceedings and power of attorney, the disputed signatures, and readiness and willingness. Having reversed a decree, the learned appellate Court was obliged to give cogent reasons on each of them. Its findings cannot be sustained in the absence of such reasons. D. Scope of interference and the appropriate order

Section 100, C.P.C. permits interference in second appeal where the decision is contrary to law, fails to determine a material issue of law, or is vitiated by a substantial error or defect in procedure that may have produced an error in the decision. The objections concerning Order XLI, Rules 17 and 31, and the statutory jurisdiction under the 2025 Act, fall within those grounds. Under sections 107 and 108, C.P.C., this Court has the powers of an appellate Court, including that of remand. Remand is not to be ordered as a matter of routine. It is justified where a material defect in the appellate adjudication requires fresh determination by the competent forum. This is such a case. The disputed questions of fact call for a considered first appellate decision, and re-appraisal of the oral evidence by this Court in second appeal would deprive the parties of the right to one full appeal on facts. Reference can be made to Meer Gul v. Raja Zafar Mehmood through legal heirs and others (2024 SCMR 1496).

For the foregoing reasons, this Regular Second Appeal is allowed and the judgment and decree dated 24.03.2026 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Sargodha, are set aside. The matter is remitted to the learned District Judge, Sargodha, who shall forthwith transmit the matter, together with the complete record, to the Special Court constituted under the Act, 2025, for decision in accordance with law. The Special Court shall decide the appeal afresh, with an opportunity of hearing to all parties, independently of any observation made herein.

No opinion has been expressed on the genuineness of the agreement to sell or on the entitlement of the appellants to specific performance, and nothing observed herein shall prejudice the merits of the case. The office shall send a copy of this judgment to the learned District Judge, Sargodha, for compliance, and intimation of compliance shall be furnished to this Court through the Deputy Registrar (Judicial). (Muhammad Sajid Mehmood Sethi) Judge Approved for reporting Judge Waseem
